_comment: Traceability catalog. One entry per sparql/<id>.rq. docs/competency-questions.md is generated from this file by scripts/build_cq_doc.py; tests/test_sparql_competency.py checks the catalog against the queries, the ontology and the tests.

questions.domain_question: Who are our patients?
questions.purpose: The simplest question a patient registry must answer; it checks that the Patient class is populated and typed.
questions.expected: 5 patients: Alice, Bob, David, Emma, John.
questions.explanation: A plain type match. It works because every patient is asserted as a Patient; nobody is a bare Person (see CQ14).

questions.domain_question: What encounters does each patient have, and in what care setting?
questions.purpose: Shows how a patient's care history hangs off Encounter, and that the setting is a controlled concept, not a string.
questions.expected: 6 encounters; David has two (Emergency 003, then Inpatient 006), everyone else one Ambulatory.
questions.explanation: The setting is read through the SKOS label of the EncounterType concept, so renaming a label changes the answer without touching data.

questions.domain_question: What is each patient diagnosed with?
questions.purpose: The core clinical question; it also confirms the one-diagnosis-record-per-patient rule (nobody shares a Diagnosis individual).
questions.expected: Alice and Bob: Diabetes; David: Migraine; Emma: Influenza; John: Hypertension.
questions.explanation: Alice and Bob both show 'Diabetes' but through two separate Diagnosis records; the shared meaning is the code (CQ04), not a shared node.

questions.domain_question: Which patients have a given condition?
questions.purpose: Identify a cohort by a standard code instead of a free-text name; the parameterised version of CQ03.
questions.expected: ICD-10 E11 gives Alice and Bob; I10 gives John; Z99 gives nobody; SNOMED 44054006 gives Alice and Bob.
questions.explanation: ?system and ?code are bound by the caller. The same cohort is reachable through ICD-10 or SNOMED because a Diagnosis can carry several codes.

questions.domain_question: What medications do we know about, and what kind of drug is each?
questions.purpose: Checks the medication model that the audit found wrong (Metformin and Insulin as analgesics).
questions.expected: Aspirin has two categories (Analgesic, Antiplatelet); Metformin and Insulin glargine are Antidiabetic; only Aspirin and Paracetamol are Analgesic.
questions.explanation: Category is data (a SKOS concept) rather than a subclass, so a drug can have several and the answer is verified against data/reference/drug_classification.csv elsewhere. (tests/test_sample_data.py checks the same categories against the reference.)

questions.domain_question: Which measurements have been recorded, for whom, and in what unit?
questions.purpose: Shows that an Observation is coded (LOINC) and carries a value with a unit.
questions.expected: Alice: HbA1c 7.2 %; John: systolic blood pressure 152.0 mm[Hg].
questions.explanation: Lab results with only text (the CBC and MRI) have no numeric value and are correctly absent.

questions.domain_question: Which practitioners took part in which encounter?
questions.purpose: Care-team membership per encounter, for doctors and nurses alike.
questions.expected: 9 pairs; Encounter001 has a doctor and a nurse, Encounter003 two doctors.
questions.explanation: Only the participatesIn direction is asserted. It is the canonical direction; the inverse is left to a reasoner.

questions.domain_question: Which doctor has which specialty?
questions.purpose: Lookup used to route a patient to the right doctor.
questions.expected: Smith: Cardiology; John: Neurology; Williams: Surgery; Kumar: Internal medicine.
questions.explanation: Nurses have no specialty and are correctly absent: the query is typed to Doctor.

questions.domain_question: Which patients have allergies, and to what?
questions.purpose: The safety-critical input to CQ10 and CQ19.
questions.expected: Bob is allergic to Amoxicillin; nobody else.
questions.explanation: An Allergy is its own node pointing at a Medication, so a medication allergy can be compared with a prescription by identity.

questions.domain_question: Which medication/allergy combinations require attention?
questions.purpose: The clinical safety rule written as a plain query, the same rule the SHACL shape enforces.
questions.expected: No rows on the sample data. After adding Amoxicillin to Bob's insulin prescription, exactly that prescription is returned.
questions.explanation: An empty answer is only meaningful if the query can be non-empty, so a mutation test inserts a real conflict and watches the query find it.

questions.domain_question: Which patients are on diabetes medication?
questions.purpose: A cohort defined by drug category, the kind of question that previously went wrong when categories were classes.
questions.expected: Alice (Metformin) and Bob (Insulin glargine).
questions.explanation: Removing Metformin's category from the graph drops Alice from the answer, proving the answer depends on the modelled fact.

questions.domain_question: Which beds belong to which department?
questions.purpose: Capacity questions need the containment chain department, ward, room, bed.
questions.expected: Cardiology: Bed1, Bed2; Neurology: Bed3; ICU: Bed4.
questions.explanation: A SPARQL property path (a/b/c) walks three links in one expression.

questions.domain_question: How many diagnoses has each doctor made?
questions.purpose: Workload reporting; the aggregate-query example.
questions.expected: Kumar 3, John 1, Smith 1.
questions.explanation: GROUP BY with COUNT, ordered by count descending.

questions.domain_question: Who are all the people in the system, whatever their role?
questions.purpose: Shows why the class hierarchy matters: nobody is asserted as Person, yet everybody is one.
questions.expected: 11 people: 4 doctors, 2 nurses, 5 patients.
questions.explanation: The query follows rdfs:subClassOf with a property path. A plain type match returns nothing, which a test demonstrates.

questions.domain_question: Which appointments have not happened yet?
questions.purpose: Scheduling follow-up; the negation example.
questions.expected: Appointment002 (Emma's neurology follow-up).
questions.explanation: FILTER NOT EXISTS: absence of a fulfilling encounter is the information. This is open-world, so it means 'no encounter is recorded', not 'none exists'.

questions.domain_question: Which observations belong to a given encounter?
questions.purpose: Ties measurements to the visit in which they were taken.
questions.expected: Encounter001 includes Observation001 (systolic blood pressure, 152.0 mm[Hg]). No other encounter has observations.
questions.explanation: The HbA1c result belongs to Alice but is not linked to Encounter004, so it is correctly absent: the data does not say it was taken there.

questions.domain_question: Which medications are associated with each patient, and who prescribed them?
questions.purpose: A medication list per patient; the join goes through Prescription because a patient is not directly linked to a drug.
questions.expected: 6 rows: Alice (Metformin), Bob (Insulin glargine), Emma (Amoxicillin, Paracetamol), John (Amlodipine, Aspirin); every row names the prescribing doctor.
questions.explanation: Dose is a property of the order, not of the drug, so it is not selected here (see dosageInstruction on Prescription).

questions.domain_question: Which observations relate to a particular condition?
questions.purpose: The ontology has no 'indicates' relation, so this asks the supportable question: which measurements were taken in the encounter where the condition was diagnosed.
questions.expected: John, Hypertension, Systolic blood pressure, 152.0. Nothing else.
questions.explanation: Co-occurrence is not causation. A clinical 'this observation indicates that condition' would need a new, evidence-bearing relation; the competency question deliberately stops at what the model can support.

questions.domain_question: Is there any prescription we should stop right now because of an allergy?
questions.purpose: A yes/no safety check suitable for a dashboard badge or a pre-release gate.
questions.expected: false on the sample data; true after the conflict is introduced.
questions.explanation: ASK returns a boolean. It is the cheapest form of CQ10 when you only need to know whether to look.

questions.domain_question: Give me everything clinically relevant about this patient as a small graph I can hand to another system.
questions.purpose: Shows CONSTRUCT as an export: the answer is RDF, not a table.
questions.expected: For PatientJohn: his diagnosis and its name, and two prescriptions with their medications.
questions.explanation: Only the shape in the CONSTRUCT template is returned, so the consumer receives a bounded subgraph rather than the whole graph.

questions.domain_question: Which patients have a medical condition of any kind?
questions.purpose: Demonstrates reasoning: the data says Diagnosis, the question says Condition.
questions.expected: On the asserted graph: no rows. With the class hierarchy applied (Diagnosis is a Condition): all 5 patients.
questions.explanation: RDF stores what was asserted. The generalisation Diagnosis-is-a-Condition is an ontology fact that must be applied (here the subclass closure; a full reasoner gives the same answer) before the query can see it.
